### *Letter XIV.*

Thirdly, God exalted the **quintessences** <note>original: *quintas essentias*; literally the "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated spiritual force extracted from the four physical elements</note> of the aforementioned elements; that is, through a kind of mystical **rectification** <note>original: *rectificatione*; an alchemical term for the process of purifying a substance through repeated distillation</note>, He separated the purer parts, from which He fashioned the heavens and the stars. Finally, the properties of **Mercury** are these: that it exists as the seat of the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture; *humidum radicale*, the essential life-fluid or "oil" thought to be the source of vitality in all living beings</term>, and that it fosters and nourishes it in all things. So that it everywhere receives all moist and cold impressions and, in turn, undergoes the actions of agents of a similar quality (namely cold and moist), and distributes them to the other parts of the body in which it lies hidden. So that it may dissolve salt and assist it in the dissolution of all solids.

These are the unique properties of the **originated principles** <term>originated principles; *principia principiata*, the physical manifestations of the three philosophical substances (Salt, Sulphur, Mercury) after they have been formed from the raw elements</term> of the highest order. In the future, we shall proceed to other things. FAREWELL.

For they testify that the intermediate powers <note>original: *facultates medias*; the specific properties or capabilities of a substance</note> of the resolutions of their principles (namely of **sulfur, salt, and mercury** <term>The *Tria Prima*, or three primary elements, which Paracelsian alchemy identifies as the base components of all matter</term>) exist as being of the same kind as those that were in the original bodies, without any distinction except that they believe them to be of a more intense degree in the principles than in the bodies. 

Yet, this identity of powers is impossible unless they retain the **substantial form** <term>original: *forma substantialis*; in Aristotelian and medieval philosophy, the essential nature or "soul" of a thing that makes it what it is</term> of the bodies, because those powers are **inseparable accidents** <note>original: *accidentia inseparabilia*; properties that are so tied to a substance that they cannot be removed without the substance itself ceasing to exist</note> always remaining in said bodies, arguing for the persistence of the substantial form. 

Indeed, if the said principles could be drawn back to their former simplicity <note>reduced to their most basic, elemental state</note>, the substantial form which they last obtained would be reduced to nothing by such a backward simplification, or would remain suspended without a subject—which is naturally impossible. Nor does it stand in the way that **generation** <note>the creation or birth of a new thing</note> cannot occur without the **destruction** <note>original: *destructio*; used here in the sense of *corruptio*, the philosophical term for the decay or passing away of an old form</note> of a form; for the **generation of one thing is the corruption of another** <note>A fundamental tenet of Aristotelian physics: matter is never lost, only transformed from one form to another</note> in mixed bodies. This is because at the very same instant that the old form is corrupted, a new one of the same degree of mixture or a more vigorous one is introduced—but never of a simpler or lesser degree of composition, such that the subject would suffer the loss of its former form. Nor can it be said that at any moment it lacked its degree of being a mixture and was drawn back to a simpler complete substantial form—a condition that is necessary for the **annihilation** <note>The total vanishing of a form into nothingness</note> of a form, which we oppose. We have said: a complete form; some substantial forms...

### *Letter XX.*

Primary or primitive multiplication, Distinguished Sir <note>original: *D. S.*, likely abbreviating *Domine Spectabilis* or a similar formal address to the recipient</note>, is that which occurs by the power and action of the aforementioned **primordial seeds**.

Secondary multiplication is that which occurs by the power and action of **particular seeds**, as can be seen at the end of the book—that is, it does not occur equally across all kingdoms. This is because **primary multiplication** is proper to **minerals**, according to which they are multiplied daily in the bowels of the earth. It also applies to **vegetables** <note>The "vegetable kingdom," meaning plants</note>, because for this reason many are also produced daily, but not so many nor so frequently and easily as minerals—especially if one is speaking of "perfected" plants and not those that arise from **decay** <term>original: *excrementis*; refers to organisms believed at the time to arise through spontaneous generation from waste or rotting matter</term>. Finally, it applies less to **animals**, because they rarely, and almost never, arise by this kind of production—at least not the "perfected" animals.

**Secondary multiplication**, however, belongs most properly to animals; yet it is frequent in plants, though not as much as in animals. Finally, it is rare, or rather...

### *Letter XXXI.*

The first difference, Distinguished Sir <note>original: *D. S.*, likely abbreviating *Domine Spectabilis*</note>, lies in the distinction of the sexes—that is, male and female—which is different in the aforementioned families. For in the animal family, since God granted all animals (at least the perfect ones) a **motive power** <note>original: *facultatem motricem*; the ability to move oneself spontaneously</note> by which they can meet and fulfill their duties, God Himself willed to give to each species a unique male and female of that same species. 

In the vegetable and mineral families, however, since the species in question lack this motive power and cannot meet or be joined by themselves, He gave to all of them a **common female**. This female is encountered everywhere and suits both families equally; therefore, she is similar to no one in species, but only in genus—specifically, the subordinate genus of the mixed <note>original: *mixti subalterno genere*; referring to substances composed of the elements that occupy a middle ground in the hierarchy of nature</note>. For that female is our **universal spirit** <term>original: *spiritus universalis*; in alchemy, the pervasive life-force or "world-soul" that acts as a universal medium or "womb" for the growth of plants and metals</term>. Therefore, however many primordial seeds <note>original: *semina primordialia*</note> there are in each region of the Elements, and however many individual beings exist in the two said families, there are just as many males—but they share only a single female common to their family.

<meta>Continuing from page 285, which established that while animals possess individual sexes, vegetables and minerals share a "common female" (the universal spirit). <page-num>286</page-num>
<header>LETTERS.</header>

---

The **Second Difference** concerns the diversity of the duties assigned to each sex. This variation is significant within the aforementioned "families" of nature, especially regarding their shared duty—that is, **copulation** <term>original: *copulationem*; the joining of male and female</term>. For animals mate of their own accord, driven solely by the impulse of the **Archeus** <term>original: *Archæi*; in alchemical philosophy, the vital force or "inner craftsman" that directs the functions of life</term> and without any need for human skill. Their innate natural appetite urges and moves them toward this; for this reason, God granted them specific organs for mating and reproduction, distinct to both the male and the female.

Vegetables, on the other hand, might seem to perform this in a similar way when their ripe fruits fall and release seeds into the **womb** <note>original: *matricem*; here referring to the earth as the receptive vessel</note> of the aforementioned female—who meets them and always greedily desires them—nevertheless, they require the help of human art <note>original: *artis auxilium*; referring here to the "art" of agriculture or gardening to ensure a successful harvest</note> to ensure this happens successfully and reliably.

Minerals, too, although they are joined without the service of art during their **primary multiplication** <note>natural growth and formation within the earth</note>, must necessarily involve the hand and work of the **Artist** <term>original: *Artistæ*; the alchemist</term> during their **secondary multiplication**—which is the process that concerns us most. Because of this, neither minerals nor vegetables possess specific organs for joining or reproduction; however, for these families, the female uses **water** as her womb and **earth** as her belly <note>original: *alvum*; the internal cavity where nourishment and growth occur</note>.

There are also differences in their specific individual duties; however, because knowledge of these contributes nothing to our current subject, we shall skip over them for the sake of brevity so that we may pursue other matters. Farewell.

### Letter XXII.

The **Third Difference** relates to the disposition and preparation of the **Universal Spirit** <term>original: *Spiritus universalis*; a vital, cosmic essence believed by alchemists to permeate the air and sustain all life and matter</term>, which must precede **multiplication** <note>In alchemy, "multiplication" refers to the process of increasing the quantity or the power of a substance, or biological reproduction</note>.

Regarding **primary multiplication** and its boundaries, there is no difficulty. No special preparation of the universal spirit is required in that instance to achieve the three boundaries, other than the degrees of **digestion** <term>original: *digestionis*; the process of being "cooked," matured, or refined by natural or vital heat</term> mentioned above. This is because it is a rule common to the three "families" [animals, vegetables, and minerals] in this method of multiplication: if the universal spirit has acquired a **sulfurous** <note>Sulfur represented the active, "burning," and masculine principle in alchemy</note> digestion while it is coupled with the primordial seeds, it is assimilated with them and turned into seed. However, if it remains at the **Mercurial** <note>Mercury represented the passive, "fluid," and feminine principle</note> degree, the species is then multiplied—that is, it is **fermented** and transformed into a specific individual according to the root and character of the primordial seeds.

But for the effect of **secondary multiplication** and its boundaries, the preparation of the aforementioned universal spirit differs greatly among the said families. In animals, it requires a further digestion beyond the preceding ones to reach the effect of the three boundaries—namely, **animal digestion**. This occurs in the **praecordia** <term>original: *præcordiis*; the internal organs, specifically the area around the heart and diaphragm thought to be the seat of vital heat</term> of animals. For this reason, God imposed upon them the necessity of **respiration** <note>breathing</note>; by the benefit of this, the said universal spirit is carried from the region of the air (where it is abundant) into the organs of the animal, where it is digested

First, by helping *Nature*, either so that it may obtain its ordinary goal of specific perfection in the things it produces—which, by a certain and unfailing law <note>original: *lege certa & indeficiente*</note>, it ought to obtain by itself without outside help, unless it were hindered and disturbed by some accident. For God, beyond the ordinary degree of specific perfection <note>original: *perfectionis specificæ gradum*; the standard level of quality or "power" inherent to a specific species or substance</note> of each being, has granted almost infinite extraordinary degrees, especially in the **vegetable** and **mineral** families. By such contraction, for example, the **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritus vini*; what we would today call ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note>—once liberated by the **distillatory art** from the huge mass of **tartar** and **phlegm** <note>In early chemistry, "phlegm" referred to the watery, tasteless part of a distillate, while "tartar" referred to the solid sediments</note> in which it is diffused—seems to be made more powerful and more advanced in its intrinsic virtue. ### Epistle XXVI.

The object of the universal gold-making <note>original: *D. S.*; likely an abbreviation for *Divinae Scientiae*, or "of the Divine Science"</note> is that **universal agent** discussed above, which must be prepared and fashioned; it is necessary to understand its essence before undertaking its production. Its definition, therefore, is as follows.

The agent used by the Philosopher for the universal transmutation of metals is gold or silver; however, the **Philosophers’ Stone** <term>original: *Lapis Philosophorum*; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</term> is gold or silver that has been **multiplied**—not in its physical quantity, but in its "seed" and in the intrinsic virtue or activity of its **substantial form** <term>original: *formæ ſubſtantialis*; the inner essence that defines what a substance is</term>, having been made most intense. This is achieved through the action of Nature and the service of Art. One tiny part of this [Stone], because of its overflowing **tincture** <term>original: *tincturam*; a concentrated spiritual or metallic essence used to transform other substances</term> or seed...

<note>original: "men"; this is the conclusion of a word split from the previous page, likely "medicamen" (medicine) or "lumen" (light/enlightenment)</note> ...[medicine], by which it is endowed with great power over any metal in various ways, able to substantially communicate the form of gold or silver and assimilate that metal to itself through a most rapid action.

*This is a standard definition:* <note>The author uses the language of Aristotelian logic, defining the Stone by its "genus" (its general category) and its "specific difference" (what makes it unique within that category).</note> for it possesses the nearest genus—namely, a golden and silvery nature—and the nearest differences—specifically, the multiplication of seed and virtue <term>original: *virtutis*; in this context, "virtue" refers to inherent medicinal or transformative power</term> (not quantity). Finally, it possesses a transmutative power over a vast quantity of any metal far beyond its own; by this, it is discerned from agents of "particular" transmutation <note>A "particular" agent in alchemy refers to a substance that can only perform a limited change, such as altering the surface color of a metal, rather than a total "universal" transformation of its essence.</note>, which transmute only a small amount, and even then only into a quantity slightly more than, or at most equal to, their own.

That gold or silver is the "genus" of the Stone, or the aforementioned universal agent, is evident from the fact that it must transmute imperfect metals into gold or silver. To achieve this effect, the natural and true form of gold or silver is necessarily required within the agent; for nothing can give or communicate that which it does not already possess.

Lest you say: "From the teaching of the first chapter, it is gathered that the Stone is the *seed* of gold or silver, and therefore not the *substance* of gold or silver"—this has already been answered there by anticipation; <note>The author argues that while the Stone acts as a "seed," it must still fundamentally be composed of the same substance it intends to create, just as a seed of wheat is essentially wheat in potential.</note>

all parts of homogeneous bodies <note>substances that are uniform in composition throughout</note> possess the same logic and nature as their whole. Therefore, the **seed of gold** is formally <note>original: *formaliter*; referring to the "substantial form" or essence that makes a thing what it is</note> gold itself, just as **vitriol** <term>a sulfate mineral; alchemists believed it could be distilled to reveal the hidden "green lion" or metallic soul</term> extracted from all other metals—which is their seed or sperm—does not differ from those metals themselves except by accident. This means it differs only by a reduction of certain non-essential qualities, such as **fusibility** <note>the ability to be melted</note> and **ductility** <note>the ability to be hammered thin</note>, and by an increase in the intensity of its essential qualities, and most especially in its level of activity.

It is said, however, disjunctively <note>meaning "one or the other"</note> that the Stone is **gold or silver**, because the Stone is twofold: one for making Gold, and the other for making Silver (although from an agent prepared for gold-making, silver can also be produced, as we shall discuss elsewhere). If the Artist aims for the first, he must establish gold as the subject of his operation, so that the Stone he creates can imprint the **golden form**. If he aims for the second, he must choose silver, so that his Stone may communicate the **silvery form**, according to the well-known axiom: *nothing can give what it does not have.* <note>original: *nihil dare potest, quod non habet*</note>

Nor is it an obstacle that some causes exist which produce effects unlike themselves—from which one might infer that gold is not necessary for making gold, and likewise for silver. This is because such a thing only occurs in **universal and equivocal causes** <note>causes that are different in kind from their effects, such as the sun's heat causing a plant to grow</note>, which are destined for various effects, in the way the heavens and stars cause things. But in **particular and univocal causes** <note>causes that produce offspring of the same species, such as a human begetting a human</note>, which necessarily produce effects similar to themselves in nature...

<summary>Sendivogius explains that the Philosophers' Stone must be made from gold or silver because a substance's "seed" shares its essential nature. ## *Letter XXVII.*

Having explained the **essence of the Stone** <note>original: *Lapidis essentia*; the fundamental nature of the Philosophers' Stone</note>, Dear Sir, it follows that we should briefly set forth its **causes** <note>original: *causas*; referring to the Aristotelian "four causes" (material, formal, efficient, and final) that explain why a thing exists</note>, because although they may seem easily judged from the aforementioned definition of terms, there remains something obscure about them that requires clarification.

And because every work presupposes a worker, we will first deal with the **efficient cause** <term>the agent or "force" that brings something into being</term>, which is either principal or ministering.

The **principal cause** is Nature herself, without whom nothing is produced that possesses natural conditions and faculties; **artificial machines** <note>original: *machinæ artificiales*; mechanical inventions like clocks or pumps</note> are not properly productions of the natural order.

The **ministering cause** is **Art** <note>original: *Ars*; here referring specifically to the "Art of Alchemy"</note>, which does not produce so much as it assists Nature in producing beyond the limits of her ordinary power, as was mentioned above.

How you shall accomplish this, however, you will learn from what follows. Farewell.

### Letter XXVIII

The **final cause** <term>the goal or purpose for which a thing is created</term> is second in the sequence, because every agent acts for a specific end; and since one cannot act for an end unless they first know what it is, we must discuss this before the others.

*The **end** <note>original: *Finis*; the intended result</note> is therefore twofold: the **proximate** <note>immediate</note> and the **remote** or ultimate. The proximate end is the first boundary of the mineral multiplication mentioned previously—namely, the preparation of the universal transmuting agent, or the multiplication of the seed of gold or silver.*

The **remote end** is the transmutation itself, in which the final boundary of the said multiplication is reached.

The **exemplary cause** <term>the model or pattern that the craftsman imitates</term> follows next. Since the Art <note>referring to alchemy</note> does not have its own unique ways of working to advance natural productions, but rather borrows those of another, it is useful to understand those methods before beginning the work. Nature’s own way of operating in its productions is the **exemplar** <note>the pattern or model</note> to be imitated in pursuing the aforementioned multiplication.

Therefore, we must consider and briefly repeat what was said in the first chapter: how **Nature** acts. Specifically, it acts by **dissolving and coagulating**. It does not dissolve by the action of fire—especially not by actual and violent fire, which does not so much dissolve as destroy and induce sterility—but rather by the impression of **mercurial water and the salt of nature**. This is achieved through the work of our **living mercury** <note>original: *mercurii vivi*; in alchemy, this refers to a specialized, "animated" form of mercury, not common quicksilver</note>, which, by means of the salt mixed into it, penetrates the salts of the bodies and the structure...

<summary>This page defines the "final cause" (the goal of alchemy) as twofold: first, creating the transmuting agent, and second, the actual transformation of metals. It also establishes Nature as the "exemplary cause" or model that the alchemist must imitate by dissolving and coagulating substances without using destructive, violent heat.</summary>

## *Letter XXIX*

The **material cause** <term>the actual substance or "stuff" from which the Stone is made</term> follows after the exemplary cause, Honored Sir <note>original: *D. S.*, likely an abbreviation for *Dignissime Soci* (Most Worthy Companion) or *Dominatio Sua* (His Lordship)</note>. This is because as soon as the artist has contemplated the idea and model of his work, he must take up the material so that he may create his work in the likeness of that Model.

It has already been sufficiently proven that **Gold** or **silver** is the material of the stone, since they have been designated as the genus and the subject of the stone which must receive its form. However, it has not yet been sufficiently explained whether the said gold or silver constitutes the **total and adequate material** <note>the complete and only ingredient</note>, or if it is only a **partial material**.

Therefore, we assert here that they are not the whole and adequate material, but only a partial one. As stated previously, the preparation of the stone is the first boundary of **mineral multiplication** <note>the process of increasing the power and quantity of the alchemical medicine</note>, which is concerned with and ends in the assimilation of something with the seed of gold or silver. Therefore, one must admit that there is something else to be used as the partial material of the stone besides gold and silver. That material, however...

...it can be no other than our **universal spirit** <term>the vital, celestial life force believed to permeate all matter</term> drawn out of our **magnesia** <term>original: *magnesia*; not the modern chemical, but a name for the "First Matter" or the raw, dark mineral ore used by alchemists</term>, because the matter from which the **seed of gold** <term>the concentrated essence of gold that allows it to "grow" or multiply</term> is multiplied, so that it may generate gold, must necessarily be **homogeneous** <note>original: *homogenea*; of the same kind or nature</note> with gold and silver. For a homogeneous thing cannot be generated from **heterogeneous** <note>original: *heterogeneis*; things of a different or incompatible nature</note> things—which is how "multiplicative gold" <note>gold that has the power to transform other metals</note> must be. Indeed, a dog or a man is not produced from a man and a dog, nor is a plant or a stone produced from a plant and a stone; and so it is with the rest.

If it should be objected that we have elsewhere accepted some partial, heterogeneous **transmutation** <term>the changing of one substance into another</term>—for instance, that any vegetable or animal food is converted into the substance of another different animal or plant, and that the same might happen with minerals.

I respond: such a transmutation is not "generation" or "multiplication" properly speaking. This is because it does not occur by the power and action of a **seed**, but is instead a "third term," or a completion of the multiplication of a generated thing, as explained above. This occurs by the power of the "scent" <note>original: *odoris*; used here to mean the subtle influence or "aura" of a substance's essential nature</note> of the **substantial form** <term>the essential identity or "soul" of a thing that makes it what it is</term> in minerals and vegetables just as much as in animals.

Nor should you insist further, by pointing out that certain offspring are produced from different animals—for instance, the mule from a horse and a donkey, and so on with others—because such offspring are **degenerate** <note>original: *degenerant*; meaning they cannot reproduce their own kind</note>; they are not of the same species as the parent, and therefore the species is not multiplied.

You will perhaps persist and say: even granted and conceded that this "second matter" must be homogeneous with gold or silver, it does not follow from this...

...that our **mercury** <term>original: *mercurium*; not the common metal, but "Philosophical Mercury," a vital fluid believed to be the life-force of metals</term> alone must be taken for the said **second matter** <term>the immediate substance used in the alchemical process, derived from the "first matter"</term>, because others are found that are equally, indeed even more, **homogeneous** <note>sharing the same essential nature</note> to the metals than the said mercury. It possesses a radical aptitude for eventually receiving that same form. This is the type of homogeneity that must exist in our second matter alongside the first—namely, gold or silver—and you will find it nowhere else except in our mercury.

The second type is that of the **principate** <note>original: *principati*; the finished or completed thing</note>, by which something agrees with another according to its final form and the conditions of its nature. In this way, gold is homogeneous [to gold]. This type of homogeneity is not required in the second matter of the **Stone** <note>the Philosophers' Stone</note>; indeed, it is contrary to its purpose. This is because the **ferment** and the **fermentable** <term>original: *fermentum* and *fermentabile*; the "ferment" acts like yeast, a small amount of "perfect" substance that transforms a larger "fermentable" mass</term> would then have the same formal degree and would not be formally distinguished from one another. But you will urge and say: this is true of gold and silver taken totally in the integrity of their substance, but not truly of their **separated principles** <note>the fundamental components, usually Mercury and Sulfur, that make up a metal</note>. Yet, the logic of the part is the same as that of the whole—that is, of the **manifested product** <term>original: *principati*; the final material result of a principle, such as a finished metal</term> however it may be destroyed. For the said principles cannot be so separated that they recover their original simplicity and totally cast off the form of the manifested product. Therefore, the same difficulty always recurs. Even if they could be simplified again, it would not contradict our position, because through that identity they would obtain the very logic of the **homogeneity of principle** <note>the state of being the same kind of "seed" or starting matter</note> that we require.

Furthermore, these principles, separated in whatever manner, would have to be restored again into the former body, identical either individually or at least specifically. This is impossible according to nature, for it would allow a **return from privation to habit** <term>original: *regressus à privatione ad habitum*; a philosophical principle stating that once a thing has lost its "habit" (its life or form), it cannot naturally return to it (e.g., a blind eye cannot naturally see again)</term>. Nor has anyone ever said that the physical parts of any substance, once separated, can be restored and reunited again into the same substance in number and species—except for man, whose **form** <note>referring here to the soul</note> is not of the material genus of forms. Farewell.

->*Letter XXX*<-

The **Instruments of the Art** of the Divine Science <note>original: *D.S.*, likely *Divinae Scientiae*</note> are vessels and small furnaces, and others of that kind, which are of two orders.

Those of the **first order** are those that serve for the **preparatory works**, and these are again divided into two classes.

Of the **first class** are those useful for the preparation of the **solvent** <note>the liquid used to dissolve solids</note>, and these are of three categories.

Of the **first category** are the vessels, namely the **Boscia** <term>original: *Boscia*; a type of bulbous glass vessel or gourd-shaped retort</term>, by which our **Magnesia** <note>original: *Magnesia*; in this context, a raw mineral substance from which mercury is extracted, not modern magnesium</note> must be distilled so that **living Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius vivus*; quicksilver</note> may be drawn out from it. A **receiver** <note>a vessel attached to the apparatus to collect the distillate</note> must be applied to the *Boscia*, and these also serve for the **rectifications** <note>repeated distillations to increase purity</note>.

Of the **second category** is the **distillation furnace** using the heat of **ashes or fine sand** <note>sand and ash baths were used to distribute heat evenly and prevent glass vessels from cracking</note>.

Of the **third category** are materials that assist the distillation, namely **cotton** <note>original: *gossypium*; used as a filter or wick</note>, or **Pumice**, which restrains the rising of the **gaseous Magnesia**.

Of the **second class** are those which are necessary for the **grinding and preparation of gold or silver**, which are also of three categories.

Of the **first category** are the vessels, namely **crucibles**, **long-necked flasks**, and **cleaning bowls**.

Of the **second category** is the **calcination furnace** <note>a furnace used to heat a substance to high temperatures to achieve oxidation or a powdered state</note> or one of open heat.

Substances of the **third category** <note>following the first two categories of preparatory tools mentioned on the previous page</note> are those that bring about the **grinding** <note>original: *contritionem*; the reduction of a solid to a fine powder</note> or **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a metal in a furnace until it is reduced to a fine, crumbly ash or "calx"</term> of gold or silver by means of actual fire. These are, namely, **corrosive waters** <note>strong acids like aqua fortis</note>, or **common Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note>, or **antimony**. It truly does not matter which of these the Artist uses, provided that he achieves a perfect grinding, so that he may clean the **ashes** <note>original: *calces*</note> of all traces of the corrosives through various washings and **reverberations** <note>original: *reverberationibus*; a process where heat is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof of a furnace onto the material</note>. This calcination and purification are entirely necessary; for otherwise, our **living Mercury** <note>the philosophical solvent</note> could not penetrate the "prisons" of the Sun <note>gold</note>, or the vitriol and the seed of gold or silver. Farewell.

## *Letter XXXII.*

The **instruments of the second principal order** are those that assist in the **cooking** <note>original: *coctioni*; the slow heating or "digestion" of the mixture</note> or **congealing** <note>original: *congelationi*; the process of the liquid matter becoming solid</note> of the Stone; these are also of three types.

Of the **first type** is a certain **glass vessel** resembling the shape of an **egg** <note>often called the "Philosophical Egg"</note>, in which both substances of the Stone must be placed—namely, **living mercury** and the **vitriol** <note>the metallic essence</note> of gold or silver in the proper proportion, which will be described later. Here, *it must be observed that the empty space of the egg should not be filled more than a third of the way, and finally, the opening of the egg should be blocked with a **Hermetic seal** <note>original: *Hermetico sigillo*; sealing a glass vessel by melting the neck shut with a torch</note>.*

Of the **second type** is an **ash-vessel** <note>original: *vas cineritium*; a container for an ash-bath, which provides a gentler, more even heat than a direct flame</note>, in which the philosophical egg must be buried and surrounded by the finest ashes to a width of at least one finger's breadth, with a hanging tripod.

Of the **third type** is the **furnace of the Stone**, or **Athanor** <term>Athanor: a specialized alchemical furnace designed to provide a constant, steady heat for weeks or months at a time without constant supervision</term>, with all its equipment. Indeed, it does not matter what kind of furnace it is, provided it maintains a very slow, continuous, and always equal...

Therefore, although all the operations can be gathered in order from our last two letters, because some details might still be lacking regarding their specific circumstances, we shall discuss them minutely.

There are two principal operations, as was stated in the article on the "exemplary cause," namely **solution** <term>solution: the process of dissolving a solid metal into a liquid state, often described as "dissecting" the metal</term> and **coagulation** <term>coagulation: the process of solidifying or thickening a liquid substance into a stable solid</term>. These, however, allow for many intermediate or preparatory steps, which are subordinate to them as means to an end, and they fall into two categories.

The first category consists of those steps prescribed for performing the **solution**, and these are of a threefold condition.

The first condition is the preparation of the **solvent** <note>the liquid agent used to break down the metals</note>, or the **distillation** of our **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: in alchemical texts, this does not refer to the chemical element magnesium, but rather to the "raw matter" or the "mother" of the Stone, often associated with lead or a dark mineral ore</term>, and the **rectification** <term>rectification: the process of purifying a liquid, such as an acid or spirit, through repeated distillation to increase its strength</term> of the same.

We specify distillation and rectification because that destructive method is useless which some **false chemists** <note>original: *Pseudo chymistæ*; a common term for "puffers" or alchemists who worked blindly without understanding the true philosophical principles</note> wish to adopt: namely, the separation of the "beginning principles" <note>original: *principiorum principiatorum*</note>—**sulfur, salt, and mercury** <note>the *Tria Prima*, the three primary components of all matter in the system of Paracelsus</note>—from one another, and their subsequent reunion. ### *Letter XXXIV.*

Once the stone is finished, there remains its multiplication unto infinity. This is performed in exactly the same manner and through the same operations as the Stone itself, except that instead of dissolved gold or silver, an amount of the perfected Stone is added equal to the amount of gold or silver originally used to create the Stone. The **Mercury** used should be no different than the one mentioned previously, but its quantity in the multiplication of the Stone is applied and proportioned in two ways.

First, ten parts of Mercury must be taken with one part of the perfected Stone. The work is then completed in ten times less time than the first creation of the Stone—specifically, in thirty or forty days. If you intend to multiply the already multiplied work again using the same proportion of materials, it will be completed ten times faster again, namely in three or four days; thus is the "work of three days" <note>a famous alchemical riddle referring to the exponential speed of the final stages of the Great Work</note> understood.

Secondly, the quantity of the same mercury is increased in a tenfold proportion, so that in the making of the stone or the aforementioned multiplication of—

In whatever way the **multiplication** <term>multiplication: the alchemical process of increasing the quantity and quality—or "potency"—of the Philosopher's Stone</term> of the stone is completed, an increase is produced not only in its physical mass, but in its power <note>original: virtutis</note> by a tenfold ratio and proportion. Thus, after the first multiplication, any part of the stone—which previously was ten times more powerful than any part of the original "seed" of gold or silver—then becomes ten times more powerful than any part of the *simple* stone, and a hundred times more powerful than any part of the said seed of gold or silver. After the second multiplication, it exceeds the stone by a thousand times and the seed by a hundred thousand times, and so on.

The reason for this is that while nature acts in the same subject toward a substantial completion, it adds ten degrees of perfection to each individual operation beyond the degree of the preceding operation, whether it produces a new and different species or takes up the same one to be improved. We could prove this with many natural examples, but you yourself through contemplation <note>original: in speculando</note> can achieve this understanding. It remains for us to speak of its use. Farewell.

[Fifth,] <note>The fifth step number is implied by the sequence starting on the previous page.</note> you should commit the closed vessel to a continuous fire of the first degree <term>Fire of the first degree: the gentlest level of alchemical heat, often compared to the warmth of a nesting bird or a slow-burning lamp.</term> to be **circulated** <term>Circulation: the process of heating a liquid so that it rises as vapor and then condenses and falls back into the same vessel, repeating the cycle.</term> for twenty-four hours over ashes. This is the **living gold** or **silver of the philosophers**, the seed of gold and silver.

The signs of a well-proceeding operation are: if the first circulation gives a golden yellowness to the liquid and, step by step in the following circulations, a redness follows; then the **Peacock’s Tail** <note>original: "cauda Pavonis"; a famous alchemical stage characterized by a shimmering play of many colors.</note>, or a rainbow or the "bow of the covenant," appears on the surface of the liquid. For this is the property of the **Vitriol** <term>Vitriol: in this context, a crystalline substance or "glass" extracted from the metal, highly prized by alchemists.</term> extracted from metals, such as our dissolved gold or silver.

Sixth, take one part of the said gold or silver, and ten parts of the **living Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii vivi"; here referring to the prepared solvent mentioned in previous steps, not common quicksilver.</note> which you set aside—or four parts if you are working with silver. This is the preparation of the **Philosophical Egg** <note>The "Egg" is the sealed container where the final transformation of the Great Work takes place.</note>.

### Letter XXXVIII.

*The particular gold-making of D.S. <note>Likely referring to the author, Michael Sendivogius (Dominus Sendivogius).</note> tends, as was said above, toward the particular conversion of any imperfect metal into a perfect one, such as into gold or silver, either according to its whole self or according to some of its parts. According to this distribution, this member is divided into two sections: The first will be concerning the transmutation of an imperfect metal according to its whole self. The second, concerning the transmutation of a metal according to some part of itself.*

The transmutation of a metal according to its whole self is twofold. The first is that which is done by a proportion of much greater inequality of the particular transmuting agent, so that one part of the agent converts many parts of the imperfect metal into gold or silver according to the nature of the **ferment** <term>Ferment: In alchemy, a small amount of a "perfect" substance (like gold or silver) added to a mixture to "leaven" or transform the entire mass into its own nature, similar to how yeast works in bread.</term>—that is, into gold if gold is provided as the ferment, or into silver if silver is substituted as the **coagulum** <note>original: "coagulo"; a substance that causes liquid to set or solidify.</note>. However, the fermentable thing is different: for in the preparation of the Stone, our mercury is taken as the fermentable thing, because it does not intend to make metal immediately, but rather the seed of the metal...

The second kind occurs by **condensation** or **fixation**, as they call it, of metals. This is properly a **sophistical change** <note>original: "mutatio sophistica"; a change that produces an imitation or "wise" deception rather than a true elemental transformation</note>, even though some metals prepared in this way may withstand many tests and examinations. This is because such metallic materials first emit their spirits into the pores of the metal that is to be fixed, through the benefit of the salts, during the first stages of heating...

### *Letter XXXIX.*

Our last letter to D. S. explained specifically and briefly those things pertaining to particular **Chrysopoeia** <term>Chrysopoeia: the alchemical art of making gold from base metals</term>, but one thing only is missing, which ought to conclude the entire treatment of the metallic art and prove the success of metallic works: namely, the method and order of **Examinations** <note>original: "Examinum"; the rigorous testing or assaying of the resulting metal to ensure it is true gold or silver</note>.

The logic and nature of examinations must come first. It must be known, therefore, that there are only two [perfect] metals, namely gold and silver, whose **fixation** <note>the process of making a substance resistant to fire and evaporation</note> is different and which obtain a different degree of perfection.

Now, there are three conditions for the perfection of both: solidity, weight, and tincture. The signs and examinations of these conditions are of two kinds: common and private.

Common tests are the eye, ignition, glowing heat, extension, the chisel, fusion, and **cupellation** <term>cupellation: a refining process where ores or alloyed metals are treated under high heat to separate noble metals like gold and silver from base metals like lead</term> <note>original: "cineritium"</note>.

The eye demonstrates the grade of the tincture to the expert Artist on the **Touchstone** <term>Touchstone: a small tablet of dark stone, such as slate or jasper, used to assay precious metals by the color of the streak they leave when rubbed upon it</term> <note>original: "Lapide Lydio"</note>.

**Ignition** <note>heating the metal until it glows</note>, if it produces a black spot in the metal being tested that covers the entire surface, is a sign of an "evil" or improper mixture.

**Extension** <note>malleability; the ability to be hammered thin</note>, if it cannot be performed, or if the metal forms cracks while being extended, indicates the addition of foreign substances in the metal, such as salts or...

...if the **antimony** <note>original: "antimonium"</note> is completely evaporated, a loss of the substance and **tincture** <note>the characteristic color and essential quality of the metal</note> occurs.

**By solution** [dissolving]: if the solution is difficult—which is a marvelous thing, as **strong water** <term>strong water: original "aqua fortis"; nitric acid, which dissolves silver</term>, which dissolves silver but not gold, once it is made into **royal water** <term>royal water: original "aqua regalis"; aqua regia, a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</term>, then dissolves gold but no longer dissolves silver—therefore, if the solution in royal water is difficult, it is proof of an enormous mixture of unchanged silver, or indeed of glass-like bodies. Finally, if the waters loaded with dissolved **calces** <term>calces: plural of "calx"; the powdery metallic residue remaining after a metal has been roasted or dissolved in acid</term> are yellow, it is a bad omen.

**By the reduction of the calces into a body** [solid metal]: if the calces cannot be reduced, or if a large part of them is turned to glass, it is a sign of the presence of foreign salts and minerals, or finally, if a lessening of the tincture occurs.

The specific and unambiguous examinations of **silver** <note>original: "argenti"</note> after **cupellation** <term>cupellation: original "cineritium"; a refining process where metals are heated in a cup of bone ash to oxidize base metals</term> are: the solution of the calces by dissolving waters, separation by means of copper plates, and the reduction of those same calces back into a solid body.

**Through solution**, a flaw is recognized if the waters loaded with calces do not have a blue color, or if the solution occurs too easily, beyond the proper measure.

**By the separation of the calces from the dissolving waters** by means of copper plates: for it is a property of true silver to adhere to these plates, a quality which does not belong to other metals. These examinations—the solution of calces, separation, and reduction—for both gold and silver, are more reliable than all others; yet they are ignorantly overlooked by assayers and are not in use among them.

<header>LETTERS <note>original: "EPISTOLÆ"</note></header>

Now follows the **Order of Examinations** <note>original: "ordo Examinum"</note>, which is threefold: direct, retrograde, and oblique.

The **Direct** [order] follows the successive series of examinations described above, including both those that are common and **equivocal** <note>tests that might apply to multiple substances</note>, as well as those that are private and **univocal** <note>specific, unambiguous tests for a single metal</note>. If the metal withstands all of these, it legitimately possesses physical reality, perfected in all its natural conditions. If, however, it does not withstand certain examinations or fails in any particular one, this occurs either in the first, middle, or final stages of testing.

If it fails in the first or middle stages—which are the common and equivocal tests—it is a sign of clearly **sophistical** <term>sophistical: in alchemy, this refers to "sophistication" or the creation of deceptive, "fake" gold or silver that looks real but lacks the essential properties</term> work.

If, however, it fails only in the final stages, it is a sign of some degree of **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a substance stable under heat so that it does not evaporate or change</term>, at least sufficient for artisanal works <note>original: "operas fabriles"; work such as jewelry or metalworking</note>. Yet that proof is not entirely certain unless all examinations are repeated three or four times in the same successive order and the metal legitimately withstands them. This is because, as we have already said, **vitrified bodies** <term>vitrified bodies: glassy substances or slag</term> mixed with metals can shield them from the first examinations; if these tests are repeated, those vitrified bodies eventually vanish and are pulled apart, allowing the metallic substance to return to its natural state. Or, if it does not return [to a pure state], that degree of fixation and perfection is insufficient, and it cannot be useful for medical works or other natural and proper duties essentially belonging to gold or silver.

The **Retrograde** order, which is shorter, begins from the final specific examinations, namely from the solution of the **calces** <term>calces: the powdery remains of a metal after it has been burned or dissolved in acid</term>, the collection, and the **reduction** <note>the process of turning the powder back into solid metal</note> of those same—

...the antimony <term>antimony: a brittle, silvery-white metalloid used in alchemy to purify gold</term> is completely evaporated <note>original: "evolatum"</note>, a loss of substance and tincture <term>tincture: in alchemy, the elusive essence or "soul" of a metal that gives it its color and properties</term> occurs.

**Through solution:** if the dissolution is difficult—and this is a marvelous thing—that *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis: "strong water," or nitric acid, which dissolves silver but leaves gold untouched</term>, which dissolves silver but not gold, once it is made "royal" <note>referring to *aqua regia*</note>, it then dissolves gold but no longer dissolves silver. Therefore, if the dissolution is difficult in *aqua regia* <term>aqua regia: "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving "noble" gold</term>, it is evidence of an enormous mixture of unchanged silver, or indeed of vitrified <term>vitrified: substances turned into a glass-like state through intense heat, making them resistant to acid</term> bodies. Finally, if the waters <note>liquid solutions</note> laden with dissolved powders <note>original: "calcibus"</note> are yellow, it is a bad omen.

**Through the reduction of powders into a body:** if the powders <note>original: "calces"; the crumbly residue left after a metal is burned or treated with acid</note> cannot be reduced <note>returned to a solid metallic state</note>, or if a large part of them becomes vitrified, it is a sign of the presence of foreign salts and minerals, or finally, it indicates a loss of the tincture.

The private and unambiguous <note>original: "univoca"; tests specific to only one substance</note> examinations for **Silver** are: after the Cupellation <term>Cupellation: a refining process where ores are heated in a shallow porous cup (cupel) to separate precious metals from lead and other impurities; also called the "ash-test" or Cineritium</term>, the solution of the powders by solvent waters, the separation by means of copper plates, and the reduction of those same powders back into a metallic body.

Through **solution**, a fault is recognized if the waters laden with the powders do not have a blue color, or if the solution occurs too easily and beyond the proper measure.

Through the **separation** of the powders from the solvent waters by means of copper plates: for it is a specific property of true silver that it adheres to the copper, a quality which other metals do not possess. These examinations, however—the solution of powders, their separation, and their reduction, for both gold and silver—are more secure than all others. And yet, they are ignorantly overlooked by many examiners and are not in common use among them.

There now follows the order of **Tests**, which is threefold: **direct**, **retrograde**, and **oblique**.

The **direct** order follows the successive series of tests described above, involving both the common and equivocal <note>tests that might apply to several different substances</note> as well as the private and unambiguous <note>tests specific to one particular metal</note>. If the metal withstands all of these, it lawfully possesses physical reality, being complete in all its natural conditions. If, however, it does not withstand some tests or falters in any, this occurs either in the first, the middle, or the final tests.

If it fails in the first and middle tests, which are common and equivocal, it is a sign of a work that is plainly sophisticated <note>original: "sophisticæ"; in alchemy, this refers to "sophistication" or the use of deceptive techniques to make a metal look like gold or silver without changing its essence</note>.

If, however, it fails only in the final tests, it is a sign of some degree of fixation <term>fixation: the process of making a substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire</term> that is at least sufficient for the works of blacksmiths; yet that proof is not entirely certain unless the metal lawfully withstands all the tests repeated three or four times in the same successive order. This is because, as we have already said, vitrified <term>vitrified: substances turned into a glass-like state through intense heat, which can shield impurities from chemical reactions</term> bodies mixed with metals can protect them from the initial tests; if the tests are repeated, those vitrified bodies eventually vanish and are dispersed, allowing the metallic substance to return to its natural state. Or, if it does not return, that fixation and perfection are merely sufficient for common use; it cannot be useful for medical works or other natural duties essentially proper to gold or silver.

The **retrograde** order, which is shorter, begins from the final unambiguous tests, namely from the solution of powders <note>original: "calcium"; the crumbly residue left after a metal has been "calcined" or burnt to a powder</note>, and the collection and reduction <note>the process of melting a powder back into a solid metallic "body"</note> of the same.

### *Letter XLII.*

The first [means] is that, for the sake of greater obscurity, they not only distribute a single matter in various parts of their writings—usually piece by piece <note>original: "membratim"</note>—but they also throw in deliberate, not to say formal, contradictions, so that what one passage asserts, another denies. However, they do not entirely suppress the logic of distinction and reconciliation; rather, they sink it under a vast and deep sea of confusion.

The second is that they often express two or even more entirely different things in the same place—that is, in the same context. Or indeed, if they distinguish them in different places and contexts, they confuse them with almost the same words apparently signifying the same thing. This is especially true when they touch upon the preparation of **mercury** <term>Mercury: In alchemy, this often refers to 'Philosophical Mercury,' the living spirit or essential substrate of matter, rather than common quicksilver</term> or its **mastery** <term>Magisterium: The specialized alchemical process or 'masterwork' required to complete a stage of the transformation</term> and its **fermentation** <term>Fermentation: The stage where the 'medicine' or 'stone' is joined with a specific metal (like gold) to 'ferment' it and give it the power to transform other metals</term>, or its specific determination toward a metallic nature. For although these processes differ as much as the heavens from the earth <note>original: "toto coelo"</note>, they make them appear so similar that propositions joined together, which seem to have a unified meaning, actually hold separate intentions, linked only by the affinity of materials, analogy, or similarity of names <note>original: "homonymia"</note>.

The third is that they strive for an inverted order, especially in the treatment of subjects and the arrangement of operations, because those things which in the correct order...

### *Epistle XLIII.*

Following a general warning regarding the reading and understanding of authors, it is helpful, Dear Friend <note>original: "D. S." likely standing for "Dilecte Socie" (Dear Associate) or "Dilecte Salve" (Dear Greetings)</note>, to proceed to a more specific explanation. This does not concern every single passage or specific contradiction regarding the final part of **Chrysopeia** <term>Chrysopeia: The alchemical art of "gold-making," from the Greek 'chrusos' (gold) and 'poiein' (to make)</term> about which you especially ask; rather, it concerns the major points. To these points, all other passages and contradictions encountered in our writings, as well as in those of other authors everywhere, can be referred for explanation and reconciliation.

Therefore, all apparent contradictions in the writings of all authors, as well as our own, revolve either around the **things** signified by terms, or around the **terms** signifying those things.

Those contradictions that revolve around the "things" are generally reduced to two main heads: namely, the **matter** <note>the physical substance or starting material</note> and the **method of operation**.

The first head <note>Matter</note> is divided into two articles, following the two major doubts: specifically, how many materials the Stone consists of, and what kind of materials they are.

The first article, which questions how many materials make up the **Stone** <term>The Philosopher's Stone: The legendary substance sought by alchemists to transmute metals and prolong life</term>: Some authors stubbornly maintain, and even constantly assert with religious solemnity, that there is only one single thing. Or, if there are several, they argue these exist and behave as parts of a lower composite or mixture—that is, considered in the sense of a mixture—of which there are only three, namely **salt**, **sulfur**, and **mercury** <note>original: "sal, sulphur & mercurius." These are the *Tria Prima* (Three Primes), the foundational elements of matter in Paracelsian alchemy</note>. These constitute only one physical whole, being a single thing in itself within any mixture, not...

<meta>This page continues a technical debate regarding whether the "principles" of matter (Mercury, Salt, and Sulphur) are the same as the substances they form. It addresses an "objection" about how these parts relate to the whole, specifically within the framework of Sendivogius's alchemical theory.</meta>

<page-num>320</page-num>
<header>MICHAEL SENDIVOGIUS</header>
<meta>catchword: infi-</meta>

...in species and number more so in the natural parts of every mixture, insofar as it is mixed—namely, by **Mercury**, **Salt**, and **Sulphur**—it will hold true, because they share the same material principle in number and species with their whole. This objection is indeed very pressing, and its solution is hardly found clearly expressed anywhere. We wish for you to receive it here.

In order to respond decisively to this objection, it must be observed that three conditions are required for a thing to be called "homogeneous" <note>Sharing the same nature or origins.</note> by the homogeneity of its principle, according to the mind of the Philosophers.

The first condition is that both must be a complete **substance**, like a part compared to its whole.

The second is that, out of those complete substances, one is in the state of a simple mixture, while the other is at least one degree further advanced on the "scale of mixtures," which we have set forth in the *Theoretical Letters* <note>Sendivogius is referring to his own written works, where he categorizes the stages of material refinement.</note>.

The third condition is that the one which is simpler must be "indifferent" to all forms <note>Meaning it has no fixed identity yet and can be molded into anything.</note>, and must be naturally capable and fit to receive the form of the other, more composed thing, anew and beyond its own nature.

Furthermore, it must be observed that the name "**root**" is equivocal <note>It has multiple meanings depending on context.</note>, and is understood in three ways.

First, it is used properly for the material principle of all things—not for that "imaginary formless matter" envisioned by the **heterodox School** <note>original: "cacodoxa Schola." Sendivogius uses this term to disparage the traditional academic or "Scholastic" philosophers of the universities who relied on abstract logic rather than chemical experimentation.</note>—but for our **universal spirit** <term>spiritus universalis: the pervasive, life-giving energy that alchemists believed could be captured and condensed into matter.</term> which is not yet "contracted" or fixed into a specific type of mixture.

<page-num>321</page-num>
<header>LETTERS.</header>

...accounted as the lowest of the complete substances, or if you prefer, for the principles which are themselves derived from even simpler principles, gradually descending to the simplest of Elements, or even the **universal primordial water** <note>original: *aquam catholicam primordialem*; in alchemy, this refers to a theoretical primary liquid from which all things in the universe were originally created.</note>.

Secondly, it is used improperly, by analogy to the previous definition, for the principal part of any living thing which first receives nourishment, which it then distributes to the other parts, either collectively or individually.

Thirdly, it is used even more improperly for any trunk or stem in relation to the parts pruned or separated from it; that is, for the whole, in any given instance, or a **complete substance** <term>substantia completa: a finished thing that can exist on its own, like a plant or a stone, rather than just an ingredient</term> in relation to its own incomplete substantial parts.

With these points established, the answer and solution to the objection is easy. For the mixtures of all three families <note>Refers to the three kingdoms of nature: Mineral, Vegetable, and Animal.</note> of every species, when compared among themselves, do indeed meet the first condition: namely, that they are complete substances and all others are lacking. They are of the same degree on the **scale of mixtures** <note>original: *scala mixtorum*; a hierarchical ranking used by Sendivogius to show how matter evolves from simple elements to complex life.</note> of the final kind—that is, under any individual species of one or another of the three families. Therefore, although they can be **transmuted** <term>transmutari: the process of changing one substance into another by altering its internal balance</term> into one another (as we have said elsewhere, one into another by the "scent" of the **substantial form** <term>forma substantialis: the core essence or "soul" of a material that gives it its specific properties</term>), they nonetheless cannot help but acquire their own form at a higher degree. However, the **salt**, **sulphur**, and **mercury** <note>The *Tria Prima*: the three base principles that alchemists believed made up all physical matter.</note> of any mixture, if they could be separated (which is denied), would not be complete substances, because they always stand as parts in relation to the whole.

### *Letter XLV.*

The second article of **Lord S.** <note>original: D.S.; likely referring to the author, Michael Sendivogius</note> deals with the quality of the matter and is divided into two Sections, following the division of the preceding article which distributed the total matter of the **Stone** <note>original: *Lapis*; the Philosopher's Stone</note> into two partial matters.

In the First Section, we deal with the doubts regarding the **first matter** <term>materia prima: in this context, the active or "male" principle that acts upon other substances</term>, that is, the active or assimilating matter.

In the Second Section, we will deal with the objections regarding the **second matter** <term>materia secunda: the passive or "female" substance that receives the form of the active principle</term>, that is, the passive matter, or the matter to be assimilated.

Both sections are again subdivided into parts, the first of which will consider the essence and nature of the matter, while the second will consider its properties.

Concerning the **first matter**, then, and its nature and essence: some say it is common and ordinary or simple **gold or silver** <note>original: *aurum vel argentum*</note>, such as is drawn from mines, and not any other substance; indeed, many passages among the Philosophers seem to prove this proposition.

### *Letter XLVII*

Regarding the properties of the **first matter**, Dear Student, there are no disagreements among authors, or at least only slight ones. Whatever these disagreements may be, they can easily be reconciled with the teachings of the preceding Letters; for this reason, let us immediately address the **second matter** <term>materia secunda: the specific material, already partially prepared by nature or art, that the alchemist chooses to begin the Great Work</term>.

Regarding the **second matter**, there are no fewer disagreements than those that came before. For some would have it be common or **vulgar mercury** <note>original: vulgarem mercurium; ordinary quicksilver</note>. The entire crowd of modern Philosophers agrees with this opinion, relying on similar arguments and the **apophthegms** <note>concise sayings or maxims</note> of the ancient wise men.

Others, being less scrupulous, affirm that the mercurial part of all things—whether mineral, vegetable, or animal—is equally useful and can be employed either collectively or individually as the second matter, because the **Mercury of the Philosophers** <term>Mercurius Philosophorum: the vital, "living" essence sought by alchemists, distinct from common liquid metal</term> is said to be in all places and in all things.

Finally, others describe it as a vile thing known to everyone, occurring everywhere, common to all people and right before their eyes; they grant their—not very sweet-smelling—support to **dung and excrement** <note>original: stercoribus & excrementis; alchemists often spoke of the "vile" or "rejected" origins of the Stone to test the student's resolve or to hide the true ingredient</note>.

In order for these opinions to be properly reconciled, we must reveal in this place a secret that is above all... <note>original: omni- (the text cuts off at the catchword for the next page)</note>

### Letter XLVIII.

Having established the secret of the preceding letter, Dear Friend, the contradictions regarding the **second matter** <note>As defined on the previous page, the specific substance chosen for the alchemical work.</note> are easily dissolved.

The first opinion, therefore, is distinguished in a twofold manner. First, by the distinction of the term or that common word; for if one deals with the very substance of the second matter—namely, our **universal spirit**—and this word is taken improperly to mean "common" (that is, signifying something ordinary and not rare), then this opinion is entirely false. If, however, the same word is taken in its proper and natural sense, as it signifies a disposition toward various things and is referred to the substance of the second matter itself, then the opinion is most true; **Mercury**...

Secondly, the same opinion is distinguished by the difference between **passive potential** and **actualization** <note>original: "Potentiæ passivæ & actus"; a classic philosophical distinction where a thing can potentially become something else (potential) or is currently that thing (act).</note>, a distinction which was applied to other substances in the preceding articles. Nor is this way of speaking unusual; for in this sense, the **wheat plant** <note>original: "herba triticaria"</note> is called "human food," even though a human does not eat the plant directly. Instead, one eats the bread made from the seed of this plant, and so it is with other things. But if [the second matter] is taken to mean actual, finished common mercury, the statement is entirely false.

### *Letter XLIX*

The second opinion, if it is understood to be about the second matter itself or its subject and its way of existing within it, is plainly false. As for the authorities that support the idea of the "first matter"—namely, regarding the **vitriol of gold** <term>vitriolum auri: a chemical salt or sulfate derived from gold; in alchemy, it often represents a purified or "opened" state of the metal.</term> or of silver—the claim that such vitriol and **metallic mercury** <term>mercurius metallicus: the essential spirit of a metal, believed to be the "seed" required for transmutation, distinct from common quicksilver.</term> in a state of **metallic decoction** <term>coctio: literally "cooking"; the alchemical process of maturing or refining a substance through steady heat.</term> are the [primary] matter, this is an unusual way of speaking. This is because they cannot be restored to the form of their former simplicity. 

For **wheaten bread** is often called "wheat," and it truly is wheat, yet it exists under a new form and a baking <note>original: "coctione," referring to the cooking process that changes the substance's nature.</note> from which it cannot be recalled so that it might serve the same effects and uses for which it was previously beneficial. For bread, however it is prepared, cannot be restored again to the quality of wheat or the flour from which it was made, so that it might be fashioned into bread of that same nature again. However, wheat that has not been fully baked into bread, but has been made into dough and **fermented** <term>fermentatio: in alchemy, the process of "leavening" a substance to multiply its power, similar to how yeast causes dough to rise.</term>, can ferment other doughy wheat that is not yet fermented. This same principle holds true in metals for the very same reason and cause, though in a somewhat different manner regarding the act of fermentation.

The third opinion, which asserts that the mercurial part <note>mercurialem: referring to the "Mercury of the Philosophers," a vital, animating spirit, not common liquid quicksilver.</note> of any compound is our **second matter** <term>materia secunda: the specific material chosen and prepared by the alchemist to begin the "Great Work" of transmutation.</term>, is most evidently false—whether it refers to the substance itself of the second matter, the subject from which it is drawn, or its mode of existing within that subject. 

However, the reasoning behind this opinion must be carefully distinguished. Regarding its location, it is certainly true that **Mercury**, or the **universal spirit** <term>spiritus universalis: a pervasive life force believed by alchemists to permeate the entire universe, acting as the bridge between mind and matter.</term>, exists everywhere. The air fills all the spaces of the world; it not only resists a vacuum everywhere but also intimately penetrates other nourishments and bodies in some way, at least through their pores. Far from contradicting us, this fact actually confirms our doctrine with an unassailable argument. ### ->Letter 50<-

Regarding the properties of the **second matter** and the qualities following its essence, there are many opinions. *Some desire a plainly liquid consistency, while others, on the contrary, want it solid. Some prefer it neither plainly liquid and fluid nor plainly solid, but of a middle consistency. Some require transparency, others opacity. Some look for a celestial color <note>original: "cœlestem colorem," likely a sky-blue or ethereal hue.</note>, others white. Some describe its taste and smell as sharp, others as sweet and pleasant. Some attribute humidity to it, others dryness. Some allow for an internal golden or even red **tincture** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a concentrated essence or pigment capable of transforming the nature and color of a substance.</term>, while others deny it. Some choose an aged matter, others fresh.* 

All these views are easily reconciled according to what has been said. For if we are discussing the actual substance of the **second matter**, it is liquid and fluid when it first begins to condense, and it is transparent...

### Letter LI.

The second chapter regarding the mode of operation follows, concerning which there are many opposing views. These all refer to the useful and useless parts of the **second matter** <note>original: "materiæ secundæ"</note> for the directors of the work toward the desired end. Although we have distinguished these matters sufficiently in our previous Letters, something must nevertheless be repeated concerning those various points in slightly different words and order, for greater clarity.

Regarding these useful and useless parts, some contend that only **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> or the mercurial part of our matter is useful; others claim only ***Sulphur***; others only ***Salt***. Others argue for a substance separated from its body or total substance, and then afterward restored and united again into that same body and total substance, once the **phlegm** and the **dead head** <term>caput mortuum: the useless, "dead" dross or residue remaining after all the essence has been distilled or extracted.</term> have been removed. To reconcile these contradictions, two kinds of parts of the complex corporeal substance—that is, of the "Physical Whole" as our matter ought to be—must be distinguished: the natural parts and the excremental parts.

***Excrements are parts of a dual nature.*** First is the **phlegm** <term>phlegma: in alchemy, this refers to the watery, tasteless, and inert part of a substance that lacks medicinal or transformative power.</term> or the portion of mercurial wateriness which, during production, exceeds the weight of nature, or the proportion exceeding the strength of the primordial or particular seeds. Because of the weakness of nature—that is, of the expulsive faculty of the seeds or the ***archaeus*** <term>archaeus: the "inner alchemist" or vital force that directs the growth and functions of a living thing or mineral.</term> moving the seeds—this exceeding portion remains mixed in locally. It does not exist as a substantial part of the mixture, but as an accidental and congested foreign body <note>original: "aggregatum & congestum accidentario corp9 alienum"</note>, until it can be expelled by the *archaeus*.

Second is the **dead head** <term>caput mortuum: the useless, "dead" dross or residue remaining after all the essence has been distilled or extracted.</term>, which is to say a superfluous portion of earthy, physical matter <note>original: "terrestris corporeitatis"</note>. Nature is either unable to expel this or keeps it like a protective bark or rind to preserve the mixture within.

The third type is a certain **fatness** <note>original: "pinguedo"</note> that forms from both the **phlegm** <term>phlegma: in alchemy, this refers to the watery, tasteless, and inert part of a substance that lacks medicinal or transformative power.</term> and the dead head. It has the appearance of a foul-smelling, poisonous oil or a harmful sulfur.

However, these waste parts do not exist in all mixtures across the board. They are absent in mixtures of the "first class" described elsewhere—specifically the basic principles, those things derived from principles, and most especially our **universal spirit** <note>original: "spiritus universalis"</note> when considered on its own. The reason for this is that their material principles are extremely simple. These spontaneously obey the **archaeus** <term>archaeus: the invisible, vital force or "inner chemist" that directs the growth and formation of all natural things.</term>—the master builder and mover—so that they never exceed or fall short in these primary mixtures. This is because the archaeus easily summons what is lacking and drives away or expels materials that might intrude. 

This is quite different in mixtures of the "second class"—that is, the three families <note>Likely referring to the three kingdoms of nature: animal, vegetable, and mineral.</note>—whose material principles, already being more composed and heavy, resist the actions and movements of the archaeus more effectively. This resistance leads to an **imbalance** <note>original: "intemperies"</note> of the mixtures, where there is either too much or too little of one quality or another. Therefore, whatever wateriness exists in these principles is entirely **mercurial** <note>original: "mercuriale"</note> and useful. Indeed, it is necessary for all creation, because within this wateriness resides the root of **fermentability** <note>original: "fermentabilitatis"</note> and the **ability to take on a body** <note>original: "corporificabilis"</note>.

The lowest mixtures, however, do admit such parts...

...waste parts <note>original: "excrementitias"</note>: but not all things, nor all things equally, nor always; for in some there is **phlegm** <term>phlegma: the watery, inert part of a substance.</term> without dregs, and in others dregs without phlegm, as in most perfect gold and in diamonds. Therefore, things of a different nature <note>original: "heterogenea"</note> cannot be dissolved.

*Natural parts are of two kinds: namely, the necessary and the accidental.* <note>original: "contingentes"</note>

*Necessary* parts are those which essentially constitute the necessary or physical whole. Their separation completely destroys the mixture, and once they are separated from each other, they can never again be joined together or returned to the same body—neither in exact identity nor even in kind—as has been proven by examples elsewhere.

Those parts, moreover, are **matter and form**, along with their preordained or subordinate natural properties. Regarding the "form," <term>form: in Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the internal principle that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "soul" of a living thing).</term> these include all the "degrees" that the **Scholastics** <note>Scholastics: medieval and early modern university philosophers who used a highly structured logical system to categorize the world.</note> call "essential," which define the substantial form. For example, in any animal, these include "animality," "corporeity" (the quality of having a body), and "substantiality," all the way up to the highest transcendental degree of "being" <note>original: "entitatis"</note>.
